1:
Who Ethan was is unsettled before the psalm begins. Delitzsch refuses the usual reconciliation, declining "the artifices by which Ethan the Ezrahite, of the tribe of Judah, is made to be one and the same person with Ethan... the Merarite, of the tribe of Levi"; the pairing with the psalm before would be justified anyway by "their common, striking coincidences with the Book of Job". Calvin admits the identity "is somewhat uncertain": if Ethan is the wise man Solomon was compared with, "the argument or subject of the poem will not agree with his time", unless he outlived Solomon. Clarke reports that the versions cannot agree either.

Two datings follow from that. Calvin supposes the psalm written over the division of the kingdom, an offence against the promise itself: "what a horrible spectacle was it to behold that kingdom, which might have flourished in unimpaired vigor, even to the end of the world, disfigured and miserably rent asunder, at the close of the life of one man!" Clarke sets it later — "it is most probable that this Psalm was composed during the captivity" — and maps its shape: the psalm "divides itself into two grand parts".

Why a lament should open by singing is answered twice, from opposite ends. Wesley makes it a precaution: the psalmist "prefaces this, lest the following complaints of present miseries should argue ingratitude for former mercies." Ellicott makes it a technique: "the art of the poet is shown in this exordium. He strikes so strongly this note of the inviolability of the Divine promise only to make the deprecation of present neglect... more striking" — adding that "this lyric purpose soon loses itself in a dirge."

Henry and Spurgeon take the singing as a duty rather than a device. Henry turns the method into counsel: "we think, when we are in trouble, that we get ease by complaining; but we do more — we get joy, by praising." Spurgeon grounds the constancy in the object — the mercies "most certainly remain the same, whether we can perceive them or not" — and draws the contrast: "sense sings but now and then, but faith is an eternal songster."

How long "for ever" is Ellicott alone questions: the Hebrew word "has properly neither the abstract idea of negation of time, nor the concrete (Christian) idea of eternity, but implies indefiniteness" — which quietly limits what the preachers build on it. On the second verse he prefers a continuous tense, "is for ever being built up", God's faithfulness being "an edifice for ever rising on foundations laid in the heavens". Clarke reads the clause as a filing: "what thou hast promised to do to the children of men on earth, thou dost register in heaven."

Augustine builds his exposition on the name. Ethan "means strong", and "no man in this world is strong, except in the hope of God's promises: for as to our own deservings, we are weak, in His mercy we are strong." On the building he presses the verb: "in such wise Thou sayest, I build, as not to destroy: for some Thou destroyest and buildest not; and some whom Thou destroyest Thou dost rebuild."

Whose covenant it is decides how the psalm can be true. Gill takes the chosen not as David "literally understood... but mystical David, the Messiah". Clarke distinguishes the covenants — one with the patriarchs, "but I have made one with David in especial relation to himself and posterity" — then argues from history that the promise cannot have meant the natural line: "David and his family are long since become extinct; none of his race has sat on the Jewish throne for more than two thousand years: but the Christ has reigned invariably since that time." Wesley reaches the same end by another route, the throne "promised upon condition, and... literally accomplished in Christ".
5:
Ellicott explains why the psalm turns from promise to praise: "having repeated the Divine promise, the poet appeals to nature and history to confirm his conviction of the enduring character of the truth and grace of God." Delitzsch supplies the pressure behind it, since "at the time of the poet the nation of the house of David was threatened with assault from violent foes". Ellicott adds that the wonders are singular in the original, "summing up all the covenant faithfulness as one great display of wonder".

Who is praising divides them. Gill lists four possibilities for the heavens — the literal skies by a figure, the church, the apostles, or "rather... the angels" — and settles on the last. Ellicott takes even the congregation of saints for the hosts above, since the term "holy ones" is used elsewhere of angels; Wesley agrees, glossing it "the whole society of angels". Henry and Spurgeon divide the two clauses between two choirs, the heavens being "the glorious inhabitants of the upper world" and the congregation "the assemblies of his saints on earth". Spurgeon divides the labour by what each choir can see: "saints above see most clearly into the heights and depths of divine love, therefore, they praise its wonders; and saints below, being conscious of their many sins, admire his faithfulness."

Henry presses the earthly half as a duty. It is "expected from God's saints on earth that they praise him; who should, if they do not?" Assembling is part of it, and the more who come the better, "it is the more like heaven". He also finds in the work a reason to want the next world, which "should make us love heaven, and long to be there, that there we shall have nothing else to do but to praise God and his wonders."

Clarke turns the same assembly into a rebuke. "In all religious assemblies the deepest reverence for God should rest upon the people. Where this does not prevail, there is no true worship." He then draws a line most would not: "while some come with a proper Scriptural boldness to the throne of grace, there are others who come into the presence of God with a reprehensible, if not sinful, boldness."

The comparison question is answered by ruling out the highest candidates. Gill concedes everything to the angels and still denies the parity: they are "holy, wise, knowing, powerful, faithful, kind, and merciful creatures, yet not to be compared with the Lord". Ellicott identifies the rivals precisely — "sons of the mighty" is "rather, sons of God — i.e., angels". Clarke widens the field to the visible universe, the Hebrew signifying "the ethereal regions, all visible or unbounded space", and turns the verse against idolatry: "can the stars, or the more distant planets, or the moon, or the sun, be likened unto God most high?"

Ellicott repunctuates the seventh verse into apposition with the sixth, so that it reads as a title: "God sublime in the council of the holy ones, And terrible among those surrounding him." On the eighth he thinks the English limps: "the Hebrew marches more grandly than the Authorised Version — Jehovah, God of Hosts, Who as Thou is mighty, Jah? And Thy faithfulness surrounds Thee."

What that surrounding faithfulness is gets two pictures. Ellicott offers the choice: "we must either think of the attendant throngs of loyal angels, or of God clothed as it were with faithfulness." Clarke takes the first and makes it a court scene — the promises "stand round his throne as the faithful servants of an eastern monarch stand round their master, waiting for the moment of their dismission to perform his will". Wesley takes the second, faithfulness lying about God "like a girdle encompassing thee", and appearing "in all thy words and works".
9:
The sea leads to Egypt by association, and Ellicott says so: "the mention of the sea has carried the poet's thoughts to the Red Sea and the deliverance from Egypt, which is represented as some huge monster conquered and crushed." Clarke argues the power from experience — "whoever has seen the sea in a storm, when its waves run what is called mountain high, must acknowledge that nothing but omnipotent power could rule its raging" — and credits God with both states, "the Author of storms and calms". Of the monster he offers a rendering: "Thou, like a hero, hast broken down Egypt." Clarke also notes a printed oddity nobody else records, an additional line carried after the eleventh verse in one of the earliest printed Hebrew Bibles.

What Tabor and Hermon are doing there divides the three who ask. Clarke takes the verse as a compass, "all the four quarters of the globe" being intended. Ellicott allows that they stand "roughly for west and east", but adds a second reason: they are named "for their prominence and importance in the landscape", and their rejoicing is better rendered "sing for joy". Wesley reads neither compass nor song, taking the mountains for "the several parts of the land of Canaan", their rejoicing being fertility — they "shall be fruitful and prosperous, and so give their inhabitants cause to rejoice".

The throne's furniture Ellicott corrects into architecture: habitation is "rather, foundation, or pillars", righteousness and judgment "support God's throne", while mercy and truth "precede — present tense, not future — Him as forerunners precede a king." Gill notes the same alternative sense, "the preparation of thy throne"; Clarke keeps the English and presses the moral, that God's government "is founded in righteousness and judgment. He knows what is right; he sees what is right; he does what is right" — and adds the consequence that gives the psalm its later force: "his decisions are all oracles, no one of them is ever reversed."

What the joyful sound is produces three answers. Clarke hears a specific trumpet: the blessed are those "spared to hear the sound of the trumpet on the morning of the jubilee, which proclaims deliverance to the captives" — and reads the following verses through the same feast. Ellicott generalises it: they are those "familiar with the shouting and music that accompanied the feasts of Israel". Gill hears the gospel instead. Wesley combines summons and presence, the blessed being those "who enjoy the presence of God and his ordinances, to which they are called by the sound of trumpets"; Spurgeon adds that "praise is a peculiarly joyful sound."

Ellicott's note on the seventeenth verse is the tile's best. Glory should be "ornament", and he draws the whole national moral out of the word: "the crown of a nation's strength is not the triumphs it wins, nor the prosperity it secures, but the spirit in which these are used. Humility, and not pride, acknowledgment of God, and not conceit in her wealth or power, was the ornament of Israel's strength, and made her greatness in her best days." Wesley reaches the same conclusion in a line — "to thee alone belongs the glory of all their valiant achievements" — and Clarke from the other side, since the people "give glory to thee, because they know that their strength cometh from the Lord of hosts".

The closing verse Ellicott turns round entirely. Instead of "the Lord is our defence" he reads "For of Jehovah is our shield, And of Israel's Holy One our king", the clauses standing "in synonymous parallelism" and the point being that "Jehovah is the source of the theocratic power" rather than its object. Gill records the same alternative — "to the Lord belongs our defence or shield" — while keeping the received sense too.
19:
Who the holy one was is both a textual and an interpretive question, and the answers do not converge. Clarke reports that the plural is read by well over a hundred manuscripts and "all the Versions": taken singly it "most probably means Samuel", taken plurally "not only Samuel, but also Nathan and Gad". Ellicott concedes the manuscripts and rejects them — "the singular is correct, referring no doubt to Nathan" — and Spurgeon agrees, "for it was to him that the word of the Lord came by night". Henry takes Nathan here and the prophets generally elsewhere, since "to all the prophets, those holy ones, he spoke in vision concerning Christ". Wesley reads the singular as a plural, "especially to Samuel and Nathan". Gill turns the preposition instead, rendering it "concerning thy Holy One" and making the subject the Messiah rather than the hearer.

Ellicott describes the form of what follows. It "is couched in oracular language" and "is introduced by a prose statement recalling the sentences in Job which introduce a fresh speaker". More consequentially, the oracle is "founded on this old prophetic passage; but while the original reference is to Solomon, here it is extended to all David's posterity" — exactly the extension the psalm will later complain has failed.

Clarke states that complaint as the reason for the whole recital: "here the psalmist begins to reason with God relative to David, his posterity, and the perpetuity of his kingdom; which promises appear now to have utterly failed, as the throne had been overturned, and all the people carried into captivity."

The help laid on the mighty one is read as an appointment. Ellicott renders it "I have placed help in a hero — i.e., I have chosen a hero as a champion for Israel"; Wesley the same, "upon a person of singular courage and wisdom". Spurgeon draws the practical conclusion: "let us lay our faith where God has laid our help." Henry notes where the choice was made — David "was chosen out of the people, not out of the princes, but the shepherds" — and on the oath that ratifies it, that "in swearing by his holiness, he swore by himself; for he will as soon cease to be as be otherwise than holy", so that "his swearing once is enough."

What the enemy cannot do is disputed on the Hebrew. Ellicott allows the received "exact", "supported by the LXX. and Vulgate, shall not get profit", but prefers another sense — "shall not surprise him" — and reports a third, "lead him astray". Wesley keeps the plainer political meaning, "not conquer him or make him tributary". Gill reads the enemy as the devil and runs through the same three senses: he could not exact more than "the law and justice of God required of him, as the sinner's surety", nor make him tributary, nor deceive him. Of the answering blow Ellicott notes only that "beat down" is "probably bray, as in a mortar".

Clarke defends the literal reading of the promise from the record. "It is worthy of remark that David was never overthrown; he finally conquered every foe that rose up against him." He lists them — Saul's persecution, Absalom's revolt, Sheba's conspiracy, the Philistine and Syrian coalitions — and finds that all of it "only tended to call forth David's skill, courage, and prowess, and to seat him more firmly on his throne."

Ellicott closes the movement by noticing a redeployment. Faithfulness and mercy, which stood earlier as God's own attendants going before him like heralds, "are here commissioned to act as a guard to David and his house". Gill draws the distinction the transfer requires: there was "no mercy shown to Christ, as the surety of his people, but he was dealt with in strict justice", while as Mediator "the special mercy of God is with him".
25:
How far the promised dominion reaches is the first disagreement. Ellicott bounds it: the sea and the rivers are "the limits of the Solomonic kingdom, the Mediterranean and the Euphrates"; Wesley reads them the same way, as "the uttermost bounds of the promised land". Delitzsch takes the opposite view — what is promised "is a world-wide dominion, not merely dominion within the compass promised in the primeval times" — while granting that the language here "is indefinite and universal". Clarke splits the difference by fulfilling it historically: David "set his hand on the sea in conquering the Philistines, and extending his empire along the coast of the Mediterranean Sea".

Ellicott then dates the psalm from a single word, and the argument is the sharpest in the chapter. The cry "Thou art my Father" is "interesting in view of the theological development in the psalter": one might take it for a quotation from a psalm of David, "were it not for the word Father, a title for the Divine Being which the national religion did not frame till the exile period." Gill, reading the same word, says only which fatherhood is meant: "not by creation, as he is the Father of angels and men; nor by adoption, as he is the Father of saints; but by generation."

The firstborn title is loosened by everyone who touches it. Clarke states the rule: "first-born is not always to be understood literally in Scripture. It often signifies simply a well-beloved, or best-beloved son." Ellicott gets the paradox out of the history — "Jesse's youngest son became the firstborn, the favourite son of God" — and extends it "to all the Davidic succession". Wesley notices the exchange of titles, "as he calls me father, so I will make him my son", and states the rule he applies throughout: these things "in some sort agree to David, but are properly accomplished in Christ".

The enduring seed is where the literal reading breaks down. Clarke: "this can apply only to the spiritual David. The posterity of David are long since extinct... but Jesus ever liveth." Gill agrees, denying it of "a race of kings from David, which ended at the Babylonish captivity".

The condition attached raises a difficulty Gill meets by grammar. Since the psalm says "if his children forsake", not if he forsakes, the failure cannot be the king's own — "which cannot be supposed of Christ, because he knew no sin" — so the children must be the spiritual seed. Delitzsch identifies the whole clause as a paraphrase of the older prophetic promise.

On the oath the two agree on its sufficiency and differ on its manner. Clarke makes the singleness the point: "I have made one determination on this head, and have bound myself by my holiness; it is impossible that I should change, and there needs no second oath." Gill treats the swearing as accommodation, "ascribed to God after the manner of men... in condescension to the weakness of his people".

What the faithful witness in heaven is divides them last. Ellicott repoints the clause — "rather, and there is a faithful witness in heaven, which the parallelism shows to be the moon" — and gives the reason: the moon "was to the Jews, as to the ancients generally, the arbiter of festivals, and the festivals were signs of the covenant, consequently that luminary might well be called a witness in heaven." Clarke reaches the moon by another road, since "by her particularly time is measured". Wesley alone looks elsewhere, taking the witness for the rainbow, "a token of God's everlasting covenant between God and every living creature". Gill keeps the moon and turns its defects into the point, since it "has its spots, and is changeable"; Clarke reads the parallel clause on the sun as "splendid and glorious! dispensing light, heat, life, and salvation to all mankind."
38:
The psalm changes direction, and Ellicott insists the change must not be softened. "God is reproached for violating the covenant", and "the boldness of this expostulation has scandalised the Jewish expositors" — but "the point of the poem, indeed, is gone if we soften down these expressions." The reason it works: "the stronger the conviction of the inviolability of God's promises, the more vehement becomes the sense of right to expostulate at their seeming violation." Spurgeon reaches the same permission pastorally: "God's actions may appear to us to be the reverse of his promises, and then our best course is to come before him in prayer and put the matter before him just as it strikes our apprehension. We are allowed to do this, for this holy and inspired man did so unrebuked."

Henry states the difficulty without pretending it is easy. "Sometimes, it is no easy thing to reconcile God's providences with his promises, and yet we are sure they are reconcilable; for God's works fulfil his word and never contradict it." The mistake would be to read the rebuke as a repeal: "we misconstrue the rebukes of Providence if we think they make void the covenant. When the great anointed one, Christ himself, was upon the cross, God seemed to have cast him off, and yet did not make void his covenant with him." Clarke puts the tension as a question: "God cannot lie to David; how is it then that his crown is profaned?"

Henry offers two datings and finds the complaint true on either: "if it was penned in Rehoboam's time, it was true as to the greatest part of the kingdom; if in Zedekiah's time, it was more remarkably true of the poor remainder." From the fallen crown he draws the lesson that "thrones and crowns are tottering things", though "there is a crown of glory reserved for Christ's spiritual seed which fadeth not away".

The blunted sword produces the tile's most interesting pair of notes, reached from opposite ends. Ellicott argues from prehistory. The Hebrew word is not edge but rock, and comparison with an older narrative "suggests that we have here a reminiscence of the stone age. The word flint for the edge of a weapon might easily survive the actual use of the implement itself" — just as "we should still speak of a foeman's steel even if... explosives entirely abolished the use of sword and bayonet." He notes what this costs the older readers, since "the ancient versions, who knew nothing of the stone or iron ages, paraphrase, by strength, or help", and calls it a case "where the condition of modern science helps us in exegesis of the Bible".

Clarke, knowing nothing of that argument, illustrates the same failure from metallurgy: "in what a perilous and hopeless situation must that soldier be who, while defending his life against his mortal foe, has his sword broken, or its edge turned!" The Gauls, he adds, "had no method of hardening iron; at every blow their swords bended."

The ruin is traced by stages. Clarke reads the land as a vineyard whose hedge is down, and names the spoilers: "the Chaldeans and the Assyrians began the ravage; the Samaritans and the Idumeans have completed it." Ellicott catches the exact reversal in the next verse: "thou hast made to cease from his brightness" means the brightness of the sun promised earlier, the throne being cast down "from being as the sun in heaven".

Whose youth was shortened divides them last. Clarke counts the reigns — "our kings have not reigned half their days", one lasting three months and dying in Egypt. Wesley makes it dynastic: "the youthful and flourishing estate of David's kingdom was very short, and reached not beyond his next successor." Gill makes it personal, but of another king: Christ "did not live out half the time of man's age".
46:
Ellicott hears in the opening cry a state of mind: with "this persistent cry", "the poet shows that faith is not extinct, though it has a sore struggle with despair." The next clause he treats as damaged, and the alternative is memorable. As it stands the Hebrew reads "Remember I how duration", "which might possibly be an incoherent sob, meaning remember how quickly I pass"; but since transposing a single letter brings it into line with "how frail I am", "it is better to adopt the change". The following question he renders bluntly: "for what vanity hast thou created all men?" Clarke asks it in his own voice — "are all the remnants of our tribes created in vain?" — and adds that unless deliverance comes soon "none of the present generations shall see thy salvation". Wesley makes the shortened time corporate, "the time of our king and kingdom, in whose name the psalmist puts up this petition".

The universality of death is an argument, not a lament. Ellicott sharpens the subject: it is not "what man" but "rather, What hero, or champion, or great man", a word used of a king — the point being that even kings die. He also corrects "the hand of the grave" to "of the underworld, hand being used for power". Wesley turns it into the plea itself: "kings and people must unavoidably die by the conditions of their natures; and therefore, Lord, do not increase our affliction."

What the enemies reproach is the real dispute. Clarke's first answer is historical: they "search into the whole history of thy people... and they find we have been disobedient and rebellious". Ellicott gives the same sense compactly — "every step taken by Israel was the subject of reproach" — while reporting the rival: "rabbinical writers connect the verse with the delay of the Messiah."

Clarke then quotes that rival, calling it a "singular turn": the enemies "have reproached the slowness of the footsteps of the feet of thy Messiah, O Lord. We have trusted in him as our great Deliverer, and have been daily in expectation of his coming: but there is no deliverer." Wesley holds both open: the anointed may be the kings of Judah, whose footsteps are "either their ways or actions, or the memorials of their ancient splendor"; or the Messiah, whom the Jews "continually expected for a long time", so that the heathen "reproached the Jews, with the vanity of this expectation". Clarke also locates where the reproach lands: the enemies, "knowing our confidence... mock us for our confidence, and blaspheme thee. This wounds my soul."

The closing blessing produces a flat contradiction about who wrote it. Clarke thinks it editorial: "this verse concludes the Third Book of the Psalter; and, I think, has been added by a later hand, as every Masoretic Bible has something of this kind at the end of each book." He gives the evidence — the verse is missing from two manuscripts, written without points in another "to show that it does not belong to the text", and set apart in three more — while conceding that "it is found in all the ancient Versions". Gill denies the whole account: "these are not the words of the copier of the Psalms, blessing God for assistance in prosecuting the work thus far, which is the sense of some Jewish writers... but of the psalmist himself."

What the blessing means they answer alike and differently. Gill has the psalmist see the resolution before he utters it, "viewing, by a spirit of prophecy, Christ rising from the dead" and so "seeing all before objected... was reconcilable to the love, covenant, and oath of God". Wesley keeps the complaint standing and blesses anyway. Clarke concedes more than either: "let him treat us as he will, his name deserves eternal praises: our affliction, though great, is less than we have deserved."
